## What Gets Calculated

  * Scheduled pricing – DeepSeek V4 Flash and Pro use each event's timestamp: legacy rates apply before `2026-08-16T16:00:00Z`, and the later rates use UTC weekday peak windows of `01:00–04:00` and `06:00–10:00` (endpoints excluded). Cache creation follows the scheduled input rate.
  * Speed pricing – `--speed auto` is the default. Unmarked usage falls back to `config.toml` detection. Pass `--speed fast` or `--speed standard` to override every recorded tier.   * Cost formula – Non-cached input uses the standard input price; cached input uses the cache-read price (falling back to the input price when missing); and output tokens are billed at the output price.   * Totals and reports – Daily, monthly, and session views display per-model breakdowns, overall totals, and optional JSON for automation.

By default, `ccusage codex` uses `--speed auto`. Codex CLI 0.144.0 and later can persist `thread_settings_applied` events in session rollouts. ccusage associates each token event with the most recent recognized setting: `service_tier = "priority"` or legacy `"fast"` is Fast, and `"default"` is Standard. This supports sessions that switch modes over time instead of applying one multiplier to the entire day or session.

Some usage remains unclassified, including older rollouts, saved headless `codex exec --json` output, and startup usage before the first persisted settings event. For only that unclassified portion, auto mode reads `config.toml` from each `CODEX_HOME` root and uses Fast when any root has `service_tier = "priority"` or legacy `service_tier = "fast"`; otherwise it uses Standard. When a model's Fast rate is unknown, ccusage reports standard pricing rather than assuming a multiplier, which may underestimate actual Fast usage.

    ccusage codex daily --speed auto
    
    # Force fast pricing
    ccusage codex daily --speed fast
    
    # Force standard pricing
    ccusage codex daily --speed standard

For rollouts written by Codex CLI 0.144.0 and later, ccusage applies recorded `thread_settings_applied` tier changes chronologically. `priority` and legacy `fast` use Fast pricing, `flex` uses Flex pricing, and `default` or `standard` uses Standard pricing. Unmarked usage falls back to `config.toml` detection. Pass `--speed standard`, `--speed flex`, or `--speed fast` to override every recorded tier.
L147: Fast and Flex pricing use model-specific multipliers only when one is available; otherwise, ccusage keeps standard pricing rather than inventing a rate.
L148:   * Legacy fallback – Early September 2025 logs that never recorded `turn_context` metadata are still included; the CLI assumes `gpt-5` for pricing so you can review the tokens even though the model tag is missing (the JSON output also marks these rows with `"isFallback": true`).
L149:   * Cost formula – Non-cached input uses the standard input price; cached input uses the cache-read price (falling back to the input price when missing); and output tokens are billed at the output price. All prices are per million tokens. Reasoning tokens may be shown for reference, but they are part of the output charge and are not billed separately.
L150:   * Totals and reports – Daily, monthly, and session views display per-model breakdowns, overall totals, and optional JSON for automation.
L151: Reports are reconstructed from retained local logs. Missing compaction usage records cannot be recovered from their markers alone, and local totals can differ from account-wide Codex usage. Pricing aliases such as `gpt-reserve` affect cost estimates, without changing token totals or revealing an unrecorded backend model.
L152: ## Environment Variables cite50†​ L153: 
L154: Variable  | Description
L155: --- | ---
L156: `CODEX_HOME`  | Override the root directory, or comma-separated directories, containing Codex homes or saved `codex exec --json` JSONL files
L157: `LOG_LEVEL`  | Adjust log verbosity (0 silent … 5 trace)
L158: When Codex emits a model alias, the CLI automatically resolves it through the LiteLLM pricing data when possible. The built-in `gpt-reserve` alias is priced as `gpt-5.6-luna`. Codex logs retain `codex-auto-review` as a routing alias rather than recording its effective model, so ccusage applies a manually curated, best-effort timeline and marks the result with `"isFallback": true`.
L159: Based on OpenAI's cite51†July 30, 2026 Auto-review migration announcement†community.openai.com , records from that date onward resolve to `gpt-5.6-luna`, while records from March 5 through July 29 resolve to `gpt-5.4`. Server-side routing or catalog overrides can still differ from this estimate.
L160: ## Speed Pricing cite52†​ L161: 
L162: By default, `ccusage codex` uses `--speed auto`. Codex CLI 0.144.0 and later can persist `thread_settings_applied` events in session rollouts. ccusage associates each token event with the most recent recognized setting. `service_tier = "priority"` or legacy `"fast"` is Fast, `"flex"` is Flex, and `"default"` or `"standard"` is Standard. This supports sessions that switch modes over time instead of applying one multiplier to the entire day or session.
L163: Some usage remains unclassified, including older rollouts, saved headless `codex exec --json` output, and startup usage before the first persisted settings event. For only that unclassified portion, auto mode reads `config.toml` from each `CODEX_HOME` root and uses Fast when any root has `service_tier = "priority"` or legacy `service_tier = "fast"`. If no root requests Fast and a root requests `service_tier = "flex"`, it uses Flex. Otherwise it uses Standard.
L164: An unsupported recorded tier is also left unclassified rather than inheriting a stale tier. Explicit `--speed standard`, `--speed flex`, and `--speed fast` override all recorded and fallback tiers.
L165: Fallback detection reads the top-level `service_tier` and lets a named profile override it only when `profile = "name"` selects that profile in `config.toml`. Inactive profiles are ignored, and a selected profile without its own tier inherits the top-level setting. If Codex selected a profile through `--profile` or another configuration file, use an explicit `--speed` for unclassified usage because ccusage cannot infer that selection from `config.toml`.
L166: Fast and Flex pricing use model-specific multipliers only when one is published. GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra, and Luna use the cite53†documented 2× API Priority rate†learn.chatgpt.com , and GPT-6 cite54†Astra†developers.openai.com , cite55†Sol†developers.openai.com , and cite56†Luna†developers.openai.com and cite57†GPT-6.1 Sol†developers.openai.com use their documented 2× Fast rates. Models listed in OpenAI's cite58†Flex pricing table†developers.openai.com use 0.5× Standard pricing, including dated and provider-qualified names.
L167: These are distinct from ChatGPT credit-consumption rates. ccusage's `costUSD` is an API-equivalent estimate, not a ChatGPT credit balance. When a model's Fast or Flex rate is unknown, ccusage reports standard pricing rather than assuming a multiplier, which may underestimate Fast usage or overestimate Flex usage.
L168: Use cite59†`pricingOverrides` to configure a model's `fastMultiplier` or `flexMultiplier`.
L169: 
L170: bash
L171: 
L172:     `# Default: use recorded tiers, then config.toml for unmarked usage
L173:     ccusage codex daily --speed auto
L174: 
L175:     # Force fast pricing
L176:     ccusage codex daily --speed fast
L177: 
L178:     # Force Flex pricing
L179:     ccusage codex daily --speed flex
L180: 
L181:     # Force standard pricing
L182:     ccusage codex daily --speed standard`
L183: ## JSON Output cite60†​ L184: 
L185: Codex focused views use the same JSON mode as the shared reports:
L186: 
L187: bash
L188: 
L189:     `ccusage codex daily --json
L190:     ccusage codex monthly --json
L191:     ccusage codex session --json`
L192: 
L193: Session JSON includes per-model breakdowns, cached token counts, `lastActivity`, and `isFallback` flags for events that required either the legacy `gpt-5` pricing fallback or the manually curated `codex-auto-review` timeline.
L194: Have feedback or ideas? cite61†Open an issue†github.com so we can improve Codex support.
L195: ## Troubleshooting cite62†​ L196: 
L197: Why are there no entries before September 2025?
L198: 
L199: OpenAI's Codex CLI started emitting `token_count` events in cite63†commit 0269096†github.com (2025-09-06). Earlier session logs simply don't contain token usage metrics, so `ccusage codex` has nothing to aggregate. If you need historic data, rerun those sessions after that Codex update.
L200: 
L201: What if some September 2025 sessions still get skipped?
L202: During the 2025-09 rollouts a few Codex builds emitted `token_count` events without the matching `turn_context` metadata, so the CLI could not determine which model generated the tokens. Those entries are ignored to avoid mispriced reports. If you encounter this, relaunch the Codex CLI to generate fresh logs—the current builds restore the missing metadata.

L100: # All Sources (Default) cite42†​ L101: 
L102: cite43†Image: ccusage daily report showing unified token usage and costs across sources L103: 
L104: ccusage aggregates every detected supported data source by default. You do not need a special `all` command or flag for the common case.
L105: ## Basic Usage cite44†​ L106: 
L107: bash
L108: 
L109:     `# Daily usage across every detected source
L110:     ccusage
L111:     ccusage daily
L112: 
L113:     # Other unified views
L114:     ccusage weekly
L115:     ccusage monthly
L116:     ccusage session`
L117: 
L118: The `--all` flag is accepted for compatibility, but it is optional because unified views are already the default.
L119: 
L120: bash
L121: 
L122:     `ccusage daily --all`
L123: 
L124: For automation, unified JSON reports can emit several report sections from one load:
L125: bash
L126: 
L127:     `ccusage daily --sections daily,monthly,session --json
L128:     ccusage daily --by-agent --json`
L129: 
L130: `--sections` accepts `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly`, and `session`. The invoked report section is always included, and table output prints each requested section as a separate table. `--by-agent` adds an `agents` array to daily, weekly, and monthly JSON rows; session rows are already source-specific.
L131: ## How Unified Views Work cite45†​ L132:

L138: Focused  | `ccusage claude daily`  | One source with source-specific options
L139:

L100: # JSON Output cite42†​ L101: 
L102: ccusage supports structured JSON output for all report types, making it easy to integrate with other tools, scripts, or applications that need to process usage data programmatically.
L103: ## Enabling JSON Output cite43†​ L104: 
L105: Add the `--json` (or `-j`) flag to any command:
L106: 
L107: bash
L108: 
L109:     `# Daily report in JSON format
L110:     ccusage daily --json
L111: 
L112:     # Monthly report in JSON format
L113:     ccusage monthly --json
L114: 
L115:     # Session report in JSON format
L116:     ccusage session --json
L117: 
L118:     # 5-hour blocks report in JSON format
L119:     ccusage blocks --json`
L120: 
L121: Use `--no-cost` with `--json` when reports should omit cost data:
L122: bash
L123: 
L124:     `ccusage daily --json --no-cost
L125:     ccusage blocks --json --no-cost`
L126: 
L127: This removes cost fields such as `totalCost`, `costUSD`, and nested `cost` values while keeping token, model, date, block, burn-rate, and projection fields.
L128: ## Unpriced Models cite44†​ L129: 
L130: When a model has no known price, its usage is charged at `0`. Table output prints a warning on stderr; JSON output records it in the data instead, so scripts and dashboards can tell "free" from "unknown":
L131:   * `totals.unpricedModels` lists the model names, sorted and deduplicated. The key is present only when at least one entry in the report had usage with no price, so `.totals.unpricedModels // []` is safe in `jq`.
L132:   * Each affected entry in `modelBreakdowns` carries `"missingPricing": true`. Priced entries omit the key.
L133: 
L134: Both fields describe pricing availability, not amounts, so `--no-cost` keeps them.
L135: 
L136: bash
L137: 
L138:     `ccusage daily --json | jq '.totals.unpricedModels // []'`
L139: json
L140: 
L141:     `{
L142:     	"totals": {
L143:     		"inputTokens": 100488,
L144:     		"outputTokens": 3994,
L145:     		"cacheCreationTokens": 0,
L146:     		"cacheReadTokens": 50688,
L147:     		"totalTokens": 155170,
L148:     		"totalCost": 0,
L149:     		"unpricedModels": ["openrouter/auto-beta"]
L150:     	}
L151:     }`
L152: Detection follows the cite38†cost mode : an entry counts as unpriced only when ccusage had to calculate its cost from tokens and found no price. In `display` mode, or in `auto` mode for an entry that carries its own stored cost, nothing is looked up, so nothing is reported. A model can therefore appear in `unpricedModels` and still show a positive cost when some of its entries carried stored costs. An absent key means no unpriced usage was detected under the selected mode, not that every price is current.
L153: Covered: `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly`, and `session` reports for every agent, including `--instances`, `--sections`, and `--by-agent`. Focused `codex` reports set `missingPricing` on the affected entries of each period's `models` map. Not covered: `blocks` and `session --id`, which have no `totals` object.
L154: 
L155: Update ccusage, or run without `--offline`, once the pricing source lists the model.
L156: 
L157: Unified reports also support JSON-oriented flags for dashboard-style consumers:
L158: bash
L159: 
L160:     `ccusage daily --sections daily,monthly,session --by-agent --json`
L161: `--sections` emits each requested unified section from one load. The invoked command's section is always included, and the top-level `totals` object remains the total for that invoked section. JSON keys are emitted with the invoked section first, then remaining sections in `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly`, `session` order, with `totals` last. `--by-agent` adds an `agents` array to daily, weekly, and monthly rows; session rows are already per-agent.

L163: 
L164:     `{
L165:     	"daily": [
L166:     		{
L167:     			"agent": "all",
L168:     			"agents": [
L169:     				{
L170:     					"agent": "claude",
L171:     					"cacheCreationTokens": 20,
L172:     					"cacheReadTokens": 30,
L173:     					"inputTokens": 500,
L174:     					"modelBreakdowns": [
L175:     						{
L176:     							"cacheCreationTokens": 20,

L100: # Daily Usage cite42†​ L101: 
L102: cite43†Image: Daily usage report showing token usage and costs by date with model breakdown L103: 
L104: Daily usage shows token usage and estimated costs aggregated by calendar date. By default, `ccusage daily` combines every detected supported data source; use `ccusage <source> daily` when you want one source.
L105: ## Basic Usage cite44†​ L106: 
L107: Show all daily usage:
L108: 
L109: bash
L110: 
L111:     `ccusage daily
L112:     # or simply:
L113:     ccusage
L114: 
L115:     # Focus on one source:
L116:     ccusage codex daily
L117:     ccusage opencode daily
L118:     ccusage amp daily
L119:     ccusage pi daily
L120:     ccusage qwen daily`
L121: 
L122: The daily command is the default, so you can omit it when running ccusage.
L123: 
L124: ## Example Output cite45†​ L125: 
L126: cite43†Image: Daily usage report showing token usage and costs by date with model breakdown L127: 
L128: ## Understanding the Columns cite46†​ L129: ### Basic Columns cite47†​ L130: 
L131:   * Date: Calendar date in YYYY-MM-DD format
L132:   * Agent: Source CLI for unified reports
L133:   * Models: Models used that day (shown as a bulleted list)
L134:   * Input: Total input tokens sent to the model
L135:   * Output: Total output tokens received from the model
L136:   * Cost (USD): Estimated cost for that day
L137: 
L138: ### Cache Columns cite48†​ L139: 
L140:   * Cache Create: Tokens used to create cache entries
L141:   * Cache Read: Tokens read from cache (typically cheaper)
L142: ### Responsive Display cite49†​ L143: 
L144: ccusage automatically adapts to your terminal width:
L145: 
L146:   * Wide terminals (≥100 chars): Shows all columns
L147:   * Narrow terminals (<100 chars): Compact mode with essential columns only
L148: 
L149: ## Command Options cite50†​ L150: ### Date Filtering cite51†​ L151: 
L152: Filter reports by date range:
L153: 
L154: bash
L155: 
L156:     `# Show usage from May 2026
L157:     ccusage daily --since 20260501 --until 20260516
L158: 
L159:     # Show last week
L160:     ccusage daily --since 20260510 --until 20260516
L161: 
L162:     # Show usage since a specific date
L163:     ccusage daily --since 20260501`
L164: ### Recent Days cite52†​ L165: 
L166: Skip the date arithmetic when you only want the days just gone:
L167: 
L168: bash
L169: 
L170:     `# Today
L171:     ccusage daily --last 1
L172: 
L173:     # The last seven days, including today
L174:     ccusage daily --last 7`
L175: 
L176: `--last` cannot be combined with `--since` or `--until`. See cite53†Command-Line Options for how it behaves on the other reports.
L177: ### Sort Order cite54†​ L178: 
L179: Control the order of dates:
L180: 
L181: bash
L182: 
L183:     `# Newest dates first (default)
L184:     ccusage daily --order desc
L185: 
L186:     # Oldest dates first
L187:     ccusage daily --order asc`
L188: ### Cost Calculation Modes cite55†​ L189: 
L190: Control how costs are calculated:
L191: 
L192: bash
L193: 
L194:     `# Use pre-calculated costs when available (default)
L195:     ccusage daily --mode auto
L196: 
L197:     # Always calculate costs from tokens
L198:     ccusage daily --mode calculate
L199: 
L200:     # Only show pre-calculated costs
L201:     ccusage daily --mode display`
L202: ### Model Breakdown cite56†​ L203: 
L204: See per-model cost breakdown:
L205: 
L206: bash
L207: 
L208:     `ccusage daily --breakdown`
L209: This shows costs split by individual models:
L210: 
L211:     `┌──────────────┬──────────────────┬────────┬─────────┬────────────┐
L212:     │ Date         │ Models           │ Input  │ Output  │ Cost (USD) │
L213:     ├──────────────┼──────────────────┼────────┼─────────┼────────────┤
L214:     │ 2026-05-16   │ opus-4-1, sonnet-4-5 │    277 │  31,456 │     $17.58 │
L215:     ├──────────────┼──────────────────┼────────┼─────────┼────────────┤
L216:     │   └─ opus-4-1  │                  │    100 │  15,000 │     $10.25 │
L217:     ├──────────────┼──────────────────┼────────┼─────────┼────────────┤
L218:     │   └─ sonnet-4-5│                  │    177 │  16,456 │      $7.33 │
L219:     └──────────────┴──────────────────┴────────┴─────────┴────────────┘`

L252: ### Offline Mode cite58†​ L253: 
L254: Use cached pricing data without network access:
L255:

L258:     `ccusage daily --offline
L259:     # or short form:
L260:     ccusage daily -O`
L261: ### Project Analysis cite59†​ L262: 
L263: Group usage by project instead of aggregating across all projects:
L264: 
L265: bash
L266: 
L267:     `# Group daily usage by project
L268:     ccusage daily --instances
L269:     ccusage daily -i`

L271:

L278:     └──────────────┴──────────────────┴────────┴─────────┴────────────┴────────────┴─────────────┴──────────┘
L279:     ┌──────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
L280:     │ Project: other-project                                                                                  │
L281:     ├──────────────┬──────────────────┬────────┬─────────┬────────────┬────────────┬─────────────┬──────────┤
L282:     │ Date         │ Models           │ Input  │ Output  │ Cache Create│ Cache Read │ Total Tokens│ Cost (USD)│
L283:     ├──────────────┼──────────────────┼────────┼─────────┼────────────┼────────────┼─────────────┼──────────┤
L284:     │ 2026-05-16   │ • opus-4-1         │    100 │  15,000 │         256│        512 │      15,868 │    $10.25│
L285:     └──────────────┴──────────────────┴────────┴─────────┴────────────┴────────────┴─────────────┴──────────┘`
L286: Filter to a specific project:
L287: 
L288: bash
L289: 
L290:     `# Show only usage from "my-project"
L291:     ccusage daily --project my-project
L292:     ccusage daily -p my-project
L293: 
L294:     # Combine with instances flag
L295:     ccusage daily --instances --project my-project`
L296: ## Common Use Cases cite60†​ L297: 
L298: ### Track Monthly Spending cite61†​ L299: 
L300: bash
L301: 
L302:     `# See May 2026 usage
L303:     ccusage daily --since 20260501 --until 20260516`
L304: 
L305: ### Find Expensive Days cite62†​ L306: 
L307: bash
L308: 
L309:     `# Sort by cost (highest first)
L310:     ccusage daily --order desc`
L311: 
L312: ### Export for Spreadsheet Analysis cite63†​ L313: 
L314: bash
L315: 
L316:     `ccusage daily --json > may-usage.json`
L317: 
L318: ### Compare Model Usage cite64†​ L319: 
L320: bash
L321: 
L322:     `# See which models you use most
L323:     ccusage daily --breakdown`
L324: ### Check Recent Activity cite65†​ L325: 
L326: bash
L327: 
L328:     `# Last 7 days
L329:     ccusage daily --since $(date -d '7 days ago' +%Y%m%d)`
L330: 
L331: ### Analyze Project Usage cite66†​ L332: 
L333: bash
L334: 
L335:     `# See usage breakdown by project
L336:     ccusage daily --instances
L337: 
L338:     # Track specific project costs
L339:     ccusage daily --project my-important-project --since 20260501
L340: 
L341:     # Compare project usage with JSON export
L342:     ccusage daily --instances --json > project-analysis.json`
L343: ### Team Usage Analysis cite67†​ L344: 
L345: Use project aliases to replace cryptic or long project directory names with readable labels:
L346: 
L347: json
L348: 
L349:     `// .ccusage/ccusage.json - Set custom project names for better reporting
L350:     {
L351:     	"commands": {
L352:     		"daily": {
L353:     			"projectAliases": "uuid-project=Frontend App,long-name=Backend API"
L354:     		}
L355:     	}
L356:     }`
L357: 
L358: The `projectAliases` setting uses a comma-separated format of `original-name=display-name` pairs. This is especially useful when:
L359:   * Your projects have UUID-based names (e.g., `a2cd99ed-a586=My App`)
L360:   * Directory names are long paths that get truncated
L361:   * You want consistent naming across team reports
L362: 
L363: bash
L364: 
L365:     `# Generate team report with readable project names
L366:     ccusage daily --instances --since 20260501
L367:     # Now shows "Frontend App" instead of "uuid-project"`
L368: ## Tips cite68†​ L369: 
L370:   1. Compact Mode: If your terminal is narrow, expand it to see all columns
L371:   2. Date Format: Use YYYYMMDD format for date filters (e.g., 20260516)
L372:   3. Regular Monitoring: Run daily reports regularly to track usage patterns
L373:   4. JSON Export: Use `--json` for creating charts or additional analysis

L100: # Session Usage cite42†​ L101: 
L102: Session usage shows usage grouped by individual conversations, threads, or sessions. `ccusage session` combines all detected supported sources; use `ccusage <source> session` to inspect one source's session format.
L103: 
L104: ## Basic Usage cite43†​ L105: 
L106: bash
L107: 
L108:     `ccusage session
L109:     ccusage codex session
L110:     ccusage opencode session
L111:     ccusage amp session
L112:     ccusage pi session
L113:     ccusage qwen session`
L114: ## Specific Session Lookup cite44†​ L115: 
L116: Query individual session details by providing a session ID:
L117: 
L118: bash
L119: 
L120:     `ccusage claude session --id <session-i d>
L121:     ccusage codex session --id <session-i d>`
L122: 
L123: This is particularly useful for:
L124: 
L125:   * Custom statuslines: Integrate specific session data into your development environment
L126:   * Programmatic usage: Extract session metrics for scripts and automation
L127:   * Detailed analysis: Get comprehensive data about a single conversation
L128: ### Examples cite45†​ L129: bash
L130: 
L131:     `# Get session data in table format
L132:     ccusage claude session --id session-abc123-def456
L133: 
L134:     # Get session data as JSON for scripting
L135:     ccusage codex session --id codex://threads/01a0bb8c-c7c0-7630-9d82-860b875930f0 --json
L136: 
L137:     # Extract just the cost using jq
L138:     ccusage codex session --id 01a0bb8c-c7c0-7630-9d82-860b875930f0 --json | jq '.totalCost'
L139: 
L140:     # Use in a custom statusline script
L141:     COST=$(ccusage claude session --id "$SESSION_ID" --json | jq '.totalCost')
L142:     echo "Current session: \$${COST}"`
L143: ### Session ID Format cite46†​ L144: 
L145: For Claude Code, session IDs are the actual filenames (without `.jsonl` extension) stored in Claude data directories. They typically look like:
L146: 
L147:   * `session-20260516-abc123-def456`
L148:   * `project-conversation-xyz789`
L149: 
L150: You can find Claude session IDs by running `ccusage claude session` and looking for the files in your Claude data directory.
L151: For Codex, use the `sessionId` from `ccusage codex session --json`. The lookup accepts that full ID, its JSONL filename with or without the extension, the trailing UUID, or a `codex://threads/<uuid>` URI. A shortened UUID is not accepted, and a UUID that matches more than one session is reported as ambiguous.

Configuration behavior:

  1. `TelegramBot.Enabled` must be `true` or the bot will not poll Telegram.
  2. `TelegramBot.Token` is the BotFather token.
  3. `TelegramBot.AllowedUserIds` should contain your numeric Telegram user ID.
  4. `TelegramBot.AllowedChatIds` is the config-managed group/forum allowlist. You can also trust a group from Telegram with `/trust` after the admin user is allowlisted.
  5. `TelegramBot.DefaultWorkingDirectory` is the fallback working directory for new sessions that do not already have a project selected.
  6. `Codex:CodexPathOverride` is the preferred place to point at a local `codex` executable if it is not on `PATH`. The app also accepts `TelegramBot:CodexExecutablePath` and `CODEX_PATH` as fallbacks.
  7. `OpenAI:ApiKey` is required for voice-note transcription.
  8. `OpenAI:Model` defaults to `whisper-1`.

  13. `CodexTelegram:InitializeOnStart` controls whether the Codex gateway initializes during startup. Leave it `true` for normal bot use.
  14. `CodexTelegram:TerminalEventHoldMilliseconds` controls how long the bot waits for late turn events after Codex reports completion.
  15. `CodexTelegram:Context:WorkingDirectory` is the default Codex working directory.
  16. `CodexTelegram:Context:ReasoningEffort` is the default reasoning effort for normal turns.
  17. `Codex:PlanMode:ReasoningEffort` is the separate default reasoning effort for plan turns.
  18. `CodexTelegram:Workspace:WorkspaceRoots` are the directories users may add as projects.
  19. `CodexTelegram:Mode` accepts `GeneralPurpose` or `Repository`; repository mode requires `CodexTelegram:RepositoryRoot`.

## First Launch Checklist

When you launch the app for the first time, work through this list in order.

  1. Make sure the `codex` CLI works in a normal terminal session.
  2. Make sure the Telegram bot token is configured.
  3. Make sure `TelegramBot.Enabled` is `true`.
  4. Start with an empty `AllowedUserIds` list only long enough to complete the setup-code capture or run `/whoami`.
  5. Put your own user ID into `AllowedUserIds`.
  6. Add any group chat IDs you want the bot to trust.

  9. Configure OpenAI only if you plan to use voice notes.

## Set Up Workspaces And Codex Defaults

Workspaces are the directories the bot considers safe and intentional for project selection.

Do this before you start using the bot seriously:

## Summary

Currently, Claude Code's working directory is determined solely by the directory from which `claude` is invoked. Other AI coding agents (e.g., Google Antigravity, OpenCode) support setting a default working directory via their `settings.json` config files.

## Request

Add a `workingDirectory` field to `~/.claude/settings.json` so users can configure a persistent default working directory without relying on shell aliases.

Example config:
    
    {
      "theme": "dark-ansi",
      "workingDirectory": "/home/user/.dev"
    }

## Use Case

Multi-agent development environments where several AI agents (Claude Code, Antigravity, Codex, etc.) collaborate on a shared project directory. Each agent should consistently start in the same workspace without requiring shell alias workarounds.

## Current Workaround

Users must add a shell alias to `.bashrc`:
    
    alias claude='cd /path/to/project && claude'

This is less clean than native config support and inconsistent with how other agents handle this.

L164: ### Cost Calculation Mode cite47†​ L165: 
L166: Choose how costs are calculated:
L167: 
L168: bash
L169: 
L170:     `# Auto mode (default) - use costUSD when available
L171:     ccusage daily --mode auto
L172: 
L173:     # Calculate mode - always calculate from tokens
L174:     ccusage daily --mode calculate
L175: 
L176:     # Display mode - only show pre-calculated costUSD
L177:     ccusage daily --mode display`
L178: ### Sort Order cite48†​ L179: 
L180: Control the ordering of results:
L181: 
L182: bash
L183: 
L184:     `# Newest first (default)
L185:     ccusage daily --order desc
L186: 
L187:     # Oldest first
L188:     ccusage daily --order asc`
L189: 
L190: ### Offline Mode cite49†​ L191: 
L192: Run without network connectivity:
L193: 
L194: bash
L195: 
L196:     `# Use cached pricing data
L197:     ccusage daily --offline
L198:     ccusage daily -O`
L199: ### Timezone cite50†​ L200: 
L201: Set the timezone for date calculations:
L202: 
L203: bash
L204: 
L205:     `# Use UTC timezone
L206:     ccusage daily --timezone UTC
L207: 
L208:     # Use specific timezone
L209:     ccusage daily --timezone America/New_York
L210:     ccusage daily -z Asia/Tokyo
L211: 
L212:     # Short alias
L213:     ccusage monthly -z Europe/London`
L214: The value must be `UTC`, another IANA timezone name, or `local` for the system timezone. An unknown name such as `Not/AZone` is rejected with a non-zero exit code instead of silently falling back to the system timezone, which can group usage under the wrong date. The same check applies to `timezone` in a cite37†configuration file .
L215: #### Timezone Effect cite51†​ L216: 
L217: The timezone affects how usage is grouped by date. For example, usage at 11 PM UTC on January 1st would appear on:
L218: 
L219:   * January 1st when `--timezone UTC`
L220:   * January 1st when `--timezone America/New_York` (6 PM EST)
L221:   * January 2nd when `--timezone Asia/Tokyo` (8 AM JST next day)
L222: ### Debug Options cite52†​ L223: 
L224: Get detailed debugging information:
L225: 
L226: bash
L227: 
L228:     `# Debug mode - show pricing mismatches and config loading
L229:     ccusage daily --debug
L230: 
L231:     # Show sample discrepancies
L232:     ccusage daily --debug --debug-samples 10`
L233: 
L234: ### Configuration File cite53†​ L235: 
L236: Use a custom configuration file:
L237: 
L238: bash
L239: 
L240:     `# Specify custom config file
L241:     ccusage daily --config ./my-config.json
L242:     ccusage monthly --config /path/to/team-config.json`
L243: 
L244: ## Command-Specific Options cite54†​ L245: ### Unified Report Options cite55†​ L246: 
L247: These options apply to `ccusage daily`, `ccusage weekly`, `ccusage monthly`, and `ccusage session` when they are aggregating all detected sources:
L248: 
L249: bash
L250: 
L251:     `# Emit several JSON report sections from one source load
L252:     ccusage daily --sections daily,monthly,session --json
L253: 
L254:     # Add per-agent breakdowns to daily, weekly, and monthly JSON rows
L255:     ccusage daily --by-agent --json`
L256: `--sections` accepts a comma-separated list of `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly`, and `session`. The invoked report section is always included. For table output, each requested section is printed as a separate table. `--by-agent` is JSON-only; session rows are already per-agent.
L257: ### Daily Command cite56†​ L258:

L260: 
L261: bash
L262: 
L263:     `# Group by project
L264:     ccusage daily --instances
L265:     ccusage daily -i
L266: 
L267:     # Filter to specific project
L268:     ccusage daily --project myproject

L295: ### Blocks Command cite59†​ L296:
